books.authorNote: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley (1797–1851) was the daughter of the philosopher William Godwin and the writer Mary Wollstonecraft. She began Frankenstein in the summer of 1816 near Geneva, during a ghost-story challenge with Lord Byron and Percy Shelley, and it was published anonymously in 1818, when she was twenty. She revised it for an 1831 edition; this is the original 1818 text. Her other novels include The Last Man (1826).

books.authorNote: Hermann Hesse (1877–1962) was a German-born novelist and poet who became a Swiss citizen. His mother was born in India and his grandfather was a missionary scholar there, and he travelled to South and Southeast Asia in 1911. Siddhartha was published in 1922. His other novels include Demian (1919), Steppenwolf (1927), and The Glass Bead Game (1943). He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946.

books.authorNote: Aeschylus (c. 525–456 BC) was an Athenian tragic poet, often called the father of Greek tragedy. The Oresteia, first performed in 458 BC, is his only trilogy to survive complete: Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers, and The Eumenides. It won first prize at the City Dionysia that year. Of the eighty or so plays he wrote, seven survive.

edition.details: Deluxe Edition, translated by Robert Fagles, introduction and notes by Bernard Knox

books.authorNote: Homer is the name given to the poet — or poets — of the Iliad and the Odyssey, the Greek epics traditionally dated to the late eighth or early seventh century BC. Almost nothing about the historical author is known with certainty; the poems were composed in a long oral tradition and later written down. They stand at the beginning of the Western literary canon, and at the beginning of my own list from Homer to Shakespeare.
